name: Tolo
catalog_quote: In Tolo the stress is nearly always placed on the next to last syllable regardless of the number of syllables in the word. For example: kuma is kú ma, but kumara is ku má ra, and bubukolo is bu bu kó lo. There are some exceptions to this. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim on the page image of printed p. vii (PDF p. 7) of the held ANU scan; locator correct. (2) Deciding source: a 1986 dictionary's pronunciation guide by a self-described non-linguist; nevertheless it is the only stress description that exists for Talise/Tolo -- Glottolog's whole bibliography is 5 items, the MED (Capell 1930, fetched sources now) is explicitly without phonetic information, Tryon & Hackman 1983 is classification/wordlists. StressTyp2 and Gordon 2002 'Penult' are downstream of Crowley. So the penult rule and dominant membership are as well sourced as this language can be. (3) What puts the STRICT coding at risk is inside the held source, beyond p. vii: Crowley marks final-stressed words with a grave in the entries, and the scanned text layer we hold drops every grave, so the sweep never saw the class. sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1930. The language of Inakona, Guadalcanar, Solomon Islands. Journal of the Polynesian Society 39(154): 113-136. (Glottolog MED for tali1259, grammar_sketch)
sources.quote: None. "No detailed information is to hand on the sounds of Inakona, but it is to be presumed that, like other Guadalcanar languages ... b and d are nasalised." The sketch is drawn 'from two handbooks published by the Mission'; no mention of accent or stress anywhere in the 24 pp. (full-text grep: only 'emphasis' in the pronoun-syntax sense).
